chicken-or-turkey-breaded-fried-caesar-g.title: Breaded Fried Chicken or Turkey Caesar Garden Salad

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of breaded fried chicken or turkey served with a Caesar garden salad – a mix of lettuce, tomatoes, cheese and no dressing. It combines crunchy meat with fresh vegetables, suitable for a light lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken and turkey belong to the same family – pheasants, but turkey generally contains less fat.
A breadcrumb coating gives the meat a golden crust while sealing in juices.
The classic Caesar salad was created in the 1920s in Mexico; this version uses only vegetables without dressing.
The cheese is usually Parmesan, rich in calcium and protein.
Skipping the dressing reduces calories while preserving the natural flavors of the ingredients.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat (especially turkey)
items.content: Turkey contains less saturated fat than chicken, which is beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals from vegetables
items.content: Lettuce and tomatoes supply vitamin C, vitamin K, and potassium, supporting immunity and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Hard cheese such as Parmesan adds calcium important for bones and teeth.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Salad greens and tomatoes provide fiber that aids healthy digestion.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken or turkey, experiencing reactions from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sodium in cheese
items.content: Hard cheeses are often high in salt; people monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Frying in breading
items.content: Frying can produce small amounts of acrylamide; cook at moderate heat and avoid over‑browning.

items.title: Caloric coating
items.content: The breadcrumb crust adds extra calories, so consider it within the overall daily intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish cold or slightly warm. Slice the fried meat into strips, toss with lettuce, tomatoes and grated cheese. Optionally add a squeeze of lemon or a light dressing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in the oven or skillet to retain crust crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: The cookie, fruit-filled bar is a soft, aromatic biscuit with a sweet fruit paste center. It weighs 45 g and is ideal for a quick snack or as a tea accompaniment.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The filling often uses natural berries and fruits without artificial colourings.
Fruit fillings trace back to medieval confectionery, where dried fruits were common.
The cookies are produced in small batches to preserve freshness and a crisp crust.
Each bar is glazed with a light coating that adds shine and extra flavour.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: The fruit filling provides vitamin C, which supports the immune system and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Contains dietary fibre
items.content: Fruits in the filling supply dietary fibre that aids normal digestion.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The bar quickly replenishes glucose stores, useful during physical or mental activity.

items.title: Low in trans‑fats
items.content: Production uses vegetable oil without trans‑fats, making the product more heart‑friendly.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The cookie contains wheat flour, so people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should avoid it.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The fruit filling and glaze increase sugar levels, so moderate consumption is advised for diabetics.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Some batches may contain preservatives and flavourings; check the label if you have specific intolerances.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The cookie can be eaten straight from the pack, broken into pieces and added to yogurt, muesli or ice cream. For a softer texture, warm briefly in the microwave for 10‑15 seconds.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a dry, cool place, in the original packaging or an airtight container. At temperatures above 25 °C the product may become soft and lose its crunch.

content.title: About
content.content: Flounder fillet is a delicate white fish meat that is commonly baked or broiled. Flounder lives in coastal waters of the Atlantic and Pacific oceans; its flesh is light‑colored, tender, and mildly sweet.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Flounder is one of the flattest fish species, with a body that lies flat on the sea floor.
It can change its coloration to blend with sand or rocks, providing camouflage.
The meat is low in fat but rich in omega‑3 fatty acids.
In haute cuisine flounder is often served with beurre blanc, lemon‑caper sauce, or in delicate soufflés.
Several species exist, including the European flounder (Platichthys flesus) and the Pacific flounder (Paralichthys californicus).

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Flounder provides a complete source of protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: EPA and DHA support cardiovascular health and brain function.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: Approximately 90 kcal per 100 g, making it suitable for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Rich in B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Contains selenium, phosphorus, and iodine, nutrients important for thyroid function and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood, including flounder.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Like many marine fish, flounder can accumulate mercury and other toxins; moderate consumption is advised.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking can allow bacterial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Flounder fillets can be baked with lemon and herbs, broiled with a light brush of oil, or steamed. They pair well with light sauces, roasted vegetables, and whole‑grain sides.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh flounder refrigerated at 0‑2 °C, wrapped in plastic, and use within 2 days. Frozen fillets store at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Before cooking, check for a fresh, mild scent; a strong ammonia odor indicates spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: The Roll multigrain hamburger bun is designed for burgers. It is made from a blend of wheat, rye, oats and sunflower seeds, giving it a fragrant taste and sturdy texture. Perfect for juicy patties, vegetables and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The Roll bun has a slightly crisp crust and a soft interior.
The multigrain blend increases fiber and vitamin content compared with regular wheat buns.
The product is baked without artificial preservatives.
Each bun weighs about 80 g.
Buns are best stored in a vented bag to maintain freshness.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: The multigrain mix provides extra dietary fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat and rye supply B1, B2 and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: May help lower cholesterol
items.content: Sunflower seeds and oats contain plant sterols that can aid in reducing LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of whole grains and protein makes the bun more filling, helping appetite control.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: The multigrain structure slows carbohydrate absorption, beneficial for stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Grain allergy
items.content: People allergic to wheat, rye or oats should avoid this bun as it may trigger reactions.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: The product contains gluten and is not suitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: The bun is lightly salted; individuals monitoring sodium intake should account for it in their daily budget.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use the Roll bun as a base for burgers, sandwiches, or as a platform for appetizers. It can be lightly toasted to enhance crunch or served cold in layered dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store buns in a cool, dry place in their original packaging or an airtight container. They can be frozen for up to 3 months; thaw at room temperature before use.

content.title: About
content.content: Stew, pork is a dish made from pieces of pork slowly cooked in a flavorful broth with vegetables and spices. The long simmering makes the meat tender and the sauce rich and aromatic. It can be served as a main course or used as a filling for sandwiches, salads, and pastas.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stewing is one of the oldest cooking methods, known already in ancient Rome.
Pork is a good source of vitamin B12, essential for nervous system health.
Stewed meat retains more nutrients than fried meat because of the low‑temperature, slow cooking process.
Traditional Russian "Stewed pork with cabbage" is cooked for over 2 hours, resulting in exceptionally soft meat.
In many cuisines pork bones are added to the broth to provide gelatin and improve sauce texture.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Pork provides high‑quality protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Stewed pork is a good source of thiamine, riboflavin and niacin, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of zinc
items.content: Zinc in pork supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Heme iron from pork is more readily absorbed than plant iron, helping prevent anemia.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Pork provides phosphorus and small amounts of calcium that contribute to bone strength.

items.title: High in saturated fat
items.content: Stewed pork can contain a notable amount of saturated fat, so people with cardiovascular concerns should watch portion sizes.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked pork may harbor pathogens such as Salmonella or Trichinella. Cook to an internal temperature of at least 71 °C.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: When soy sauce, salt, or prepared broths are added, sodium levels can be high, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Although rare, some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pork proteins.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot with a side of potatoes, rice, or vegetables. It is also used as a filling for tacos, mixed into green salads, or tossed with pasta. Chilled leftovers can be sliced thin for sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked stew in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 2–3 months. Reheat thoroughly to a boil before consuming to eliminate any bacteria.
